The 75 bp hike to 3.75–4% and continued balance-sheet runoff keep policy clearly restrictive and inflation-focused. The latest SLOOS corroborates a material tightening in credit supply and softer demand: banks reported tighter standards across C&I (including for small, middle-market, and large firms) and CRE (construction/land development, nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily), broader tightening in residential real estate and consumer credit (including credit cards), reduced approval likelihood for lower FICO borrowers (620/680) with preference for higher scores, and weaker loan demand from firms and consumers (notably credit card and auto), with some offset from stronger HELOC demand. Banks cited a weaker economic outlook and raised recession likelihood. These survey signals of tighter bank intermediation and weaker credit demand reinforce the Committee’s new emphasis on cumulative tightening and policy lags, arguing for more caution on the pace of future hikes even as inflation risks remain paramount. Net takeaway: still hawkish, but more constrained by tightening credit conditions and increasingly data-dependent.
